events/1292_brunetto/phases/0/transition: Boccaccio turns a page and stops.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/0/announceme:
We don't actually know how Dante came to know Brunetto Latini. No school record, no contract, not one letter.
There is only one reason we know of this teacher at all — Dante wrote him into the Inferno.
Hold on to that: the evidence for the real half comes from the literary half.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/0/dufu_react:
So today's lesson runs backwards.
First see how the two of them got on in this world — then see where the student put his teacher.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/narrative: Two years after Beatrice died. Dante is twenty-seven and has buried himself in books. The most learned old man in the city is Brunetto Latini — notary, former chancellor of the commune, the man who taught this city how to speak and how to argue politics.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/instructio: Talk with the teacher. Look at the two books on his desk.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/npcs/0/dia: Writing poems is no great skill, boy. This city has more men who write poems than men who read them.
The skill is this: making a whole city understand you. Rhetoric is not decoration, it is politics. If you want to go into politics, first learn how to get your words inside other people's hearts.

A man's life is short. But a man can make himself immortal — by leaving behind something that outlives him.
You don't understand me yet. You will.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/npcs/1/dia: The Trésor · Li Livres dou Trésor
The big book of the teacher's life: an encyclopedia meant to hold all the learning in the world. Astronomy, history, ethics, rhetoric, how to govern a city — all of it.
After Montaperti I was exiled to France. I wrote it in those six years. French goes further, more people read it. Learning that can't travel isn't learning.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/npcs/2/dia: Beside it, a thin one: verse in everyday Italian. In the poem the author loses his way in a wood, meets a goddess, and is led on a tour of the reasons behind all things.
…Lost in a wood. Led along by someone.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/1/npcs/3/dia: The master is old now. You've come late — he's been back from France nearly thirty years.
The whole city has been taught by him. They say he's the one who took the Florentines “from rough to fine.”
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/narrative: The teacher's big book is in French, his small one in the everyday tongue. One day Dante will have to choose too.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/question: To write a book that outlives you, which language should you use?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/options/0/: Latin — the scholars' language, the most respectable
Respectable. But your mother can't read it. Your neighbour can't read it. Who are you writing for?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/options/1/: French — like my teacher, it travels far

That is what I chose. More people do read it.
…Only, it isn't the language I was born speaking.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/options/2/: The everyday tongue — the talk I learned in the streets of Florence

If a thing is to outlive me, it has to be written in a living language.
Latin is dead. French is not mine.
I will write a book anyone can read, in the language my mother taught me.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/2/conclusion:
In 1292 this choice is still only talk. A dozen years later a penniless man in exile will use it to write a long poem in interlocking three-line rhyme — in the “everyday tongue,” not in any respectable language. That poem went on to turn that “everyday tongue” into Italian.
His teacher chose the other road.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/3/token/deta: 1292 · Brunetto Latini, who taught him rhetoric, politics, and “how a man makes himself immortal”
events/1292_brunetto/phases/3/afterText:
Seventh circle, third ring.
Fire falls like rain on the sand, and has fallen forever.
A band of souls comes along the bank, squinting up at him.
One of them suddenly catches him by the hem.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/recognitio:
The fire has scorched the face past recognising.
Dante bends down and stares a long time before he knows him —

“Are you here, Ser Brunetto?”
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/0/q: You look up to him. Why is he here?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/0/a:
Because respect does not cancel the sin.
I sentenced him to the ring for sins “against nature.” It is the hardest passage in the whole book to write.
If I moved a man somewhere he doesn't belong just because I loved him —
then this whole Hell is worth nothing.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/1/q: Then why do you still address him as “voi,” the respectful you?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/1/a:
In the whole book there are fewer than five souls I say “voi” to.
I am the one who sentenced him and I am the one who honours him. I don't intend to make those two agree.
You heard that line just now — “you taught me how a man makes himself immortal.”
That is not politeness. That is what I owe him.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/2/q: What did he say for himself?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/2/a:
Not one word in his own defence.
He asked for one thing only: his Trésor.
“Let my Trésor be left in your care — in that book I am still alive.”
Then he ran off. Like the men racing for the green cloth at Verona —
and he still looked like the one who wins, not the one who loses.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/3/q: Writing him in here — is that punishing him, or saving him?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/asks/3/a:
Decide for yourself.
Seven hundred years have gone by. People remember Brunetto Latini,
not because of that Trésor in French —
but because I put him under the rain of fire.
The “immortality” he wanted, I gave him. This is how.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/4/closing:
He taught Dante how a man makes himself immortal.
Dante did it — and took his teacher in with him.

A real teacher became a soul in Inferno XV.
That is how the Divine Comedy was built: he put the people he knew into it, one by one.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/quote:
“If you follow your star, you cannot fail to reach a glorious harbour…
But that ungrateful, spiteful people will turn against you for the good you do.
Keep clear of them.”
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/instructio: Don't read on yet. Put each of these three times where it belongs.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/axis/0/lab:
Brunetto says this
(time inside the story)
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/axis/2/lab:
Dante writes the passage
(the author's time)
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/blocks/1/t:
January 1302
Tried in absence, exiled for life
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/blocks/2/t:
Sometime in the 1310s
In exile, under other men's roofs
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/question: So is this a prophecy, or a memory?
events/1292_brunetto/phases/5/conclusion:
Brunetto thinks he is talking about the future.
By the time Dante wrote it, that “future” was more than ten years past.

He has a man in his book “foretell” suffering he had already been through.
So every prophecy in the Comedy is doubled:
the character looks forward, the author looks back, and the two lines of sight collide at the year 1300.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/6/transition: At the lectern, Boccaccio closes Canto XV.
events/1292_brunetto/phases/6/dufu_react:
For six hundred years scholars have argued about one thing:
what sin “against nature” did Brunetto actually commit?
Some say a sin of the body. Others say —
he turned his back on his own mother tongue and wrote the book of his life in French.

Which answer is right, we don't know.
But notice this: the man who sentenced him is exactly the man who decided to write in his mother tongue.
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/0/question: The Trésor, the big book of Brunetto Latini's life — what language was it written in?
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/0/explanation: After the defeat at Montaperti, Brunetto went into exile in France, and there wrote the encyclopedic Trésor in French — his reason was that French goes further. He also wrote a verse book in everyday Italian, the Tesoretto, but a much slighter one. That choice later became one of the keys to reading Inferno XV.
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/1/question: When Dante meets Brunetto again in the Inferno, he does something he does for only a handful of souls in the whole book. What?
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/1/options/3: Pulls him out of the rain of fire
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/1/explanation: In the whole poem there are no more than five souls Dante addresses with the respectful voi. He sentenced his teacher to Hell and still spoke to him with the respectful form — the verdict and the respect hold at the same time, and that is the hardest thing about this canto.
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/2/question:
Inferno XV, what Dante says to his teacher:
“You taught me how a man makes himself ___”
quiz/1292_brunetto/quizzes/2/explanation: “m'insegnavate come l'uom s'etterna” — you taught me how a man makes himself immortal. Brunetto taught him that; and the way Dante made his teacher immortal was to write him into the seventh circle, under the rain of fire.
